claims.text: The target material is homogenized, single-phase equiatomic FeNiCrMn with minimal secondary phases or precipitates.
Removing Co intrinsically lowers the stacking-fault energy of equiatomic FeNiCrMn relative to comparable Co-containing alloys.
Deformation twinning becomes the dominant dynamic deformation mechanism in FeNiCrMn at low temperature and high strain rate.
Twinning operating with dislocation glide allows FeNiCrMn to maintain a strength–ductility balance across temperature and strain-rate regimes.
At higher temperatures or lower strain rates, dislocation glide accompanied by enhanced dynamic recovery predominates.
Testing at approximately 100, 300, and 500 K and strain rates from 10^-3 to 10^3 s^-1 is proposed to distinguish twinning from dislocation-glide regimes.
In situ TEM and digital image correlation are proposed to track twin density, dislocation structures, and strain localization.
Deformation twins nucleate and propagate during deformation and interact with dislocation networks.
Limited atomic mobility at low temperature and high strain rate facilitates deformation twinning in low-stacking-fault-energy FeNiCrMn.
Twin boundaries provide additional barriers to dislocation motion.
The obstruction of dislocation motion by twins enhances work hardening.
Twinning-mediated work hardening helps preserve ductility.
Greater atomic mobility at higher temperature suppresses twinning and favors dislocation glide with dynamic recovery.
The low-temperature, high-strain-rate regime will exhibit higher twin density than the elevated-temperature, low-strain-rate regime.
The twin-dominated regime will exhibit higher flow stress.
The twin-dominated regime will exhibit enhanced work hardening.
Comparable Co-containing equiatomic alloys do not exhibit as pronounced a twinning response under the same conditions.
Co-containing equiatomic alloys show predominantly dislocation-mediated plasticity, less pronounced work hardening, and lower twin density than FeNiCrMn under similar conditions.
Impurities, secondary phases, and processing-induced defects can alter effective stacking-fault energy and cause deviations from the proposed behavior.

Failure to observe a statistically significant increase in twinning at low temperature and high strain rate, or failure to observe the predicted mechanical transition relative to Co-containing controls, would reject the hypothesis.
